item.title: American Hiker Dies After Lightning Strike on Mount Etna in Italy
item.description:
An American man died after being struck by lightning while hiking on Mount Etna in Italy, emergency officials said on Monday.

Rescuers found the 29-year-old man in serious condition on Sunday on the eastern side of Mount Etna, Europe’s largest active volcano, the local fire department said in a statement. Firefighters transported him by helicopter to Cannizzaro Hospital in Catania, the nearest major city, on the east coast of Sicily.

The hospital declined to identify the man until its officials had contacted his next of kin. He arrived in a state of cardiac arrest and was declared dead about an hour later, hospital officials said in a statement.

According to local fire officials, the hiker was found alone in an area known as Valle del Bove that was closed to the public. The valley had been rocked by an unusually heavy bout of volcanic activity in recent days, prompting the local authorities to close some of the area.

On Monday, Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology reported that another volcanic vent had opened in the valley, with fresh lava flowing overnight.

The international airport in Catania said early Monday that it was imposing limits on the number of flights arriving until Tuesday afternoon as a result of the volume of ash being released into the atmosphere by Mount Etna. Seismic activity at the volcano — which is just 30 miles, or about 48 kilometers, from the airport — had forced hundreds of cancellations and delays for more than 10 days.

While thunderstorms had been forecast for Sicily on Sunday, lightning can be generated by volcanic eruptions, according to the National Weather Service. During a volcanic eruption, tiny collisions among the rising particles of ash can create static electricity, which may in turn produce volcanic lightning. During an eruption of Mount Etna in August 2023, Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology reported lightning within the ash clouds.

According to the Italian health authorities, lightning strikes in the country are particularly common in July and August. A recent study showed that some 89 people were killed by lightning strikes in Italy from 2001 to 2020.

During thunderstorms, people in elevated areas such as mountain ridges and summits can be particularly exposed to lightning, according to the National Weather Service.

The U.S. consulate in Naples, which has jurisdiction over the region of Sicily, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nazaneen Ghaffar contributed reporting.

item.title: The Tragic Story of Jason Arday
item.description:
If ever a story seemed tailor-made to pour fuel on the culture war fires, it was the tragic story of Jason Arday.

The Cambridge professor recently resigned under scrutiny, and was found dead last week in a South London home. His story touches on deeply divisive topics, from race to higher education to D.E.I. to autism. There’s so much to unpack. To make sense of it all, I spoke to my colleague Mara Hvistendahl, who’s been reporting on Arday’s life, his death and the fallout at Cambridge.

Three years ago, Jason Arday, then 37, was hired as a professor at Cambridge University. Cambridge made a big deal of its new star, touting him as its youngest Black professor and promoting his incredible personal story of growing up in public housing and overcoming severe developmental delays to go on to academia.

Then, last month, a blog post — written by a former Cambridge researcher once disciplined after arguing Black people couldn’t succeed in a meritocracy — accused Arday of plagiarism and embellishing his life story. A firestorm ensued. British media, especially British conservative media, found the story irresistible.

Eventually, Arday resigned, saying he no longer wished to feel as if he was “living under a constant spotlight.” Last week, he was found dead in a London apartment; in a statement, his family referenced the “campaign of sustained abuse” he’d endured.

You can read my conversation with Mara below.

So, Mara. How did Jason Arday end up at Cambridge?

He was hired for an enormously prestigious position — an established chair of education — in 2023. At the time, Cambridge was under a lot of pressure to increase its representation of people of color both among faculty members and students. And you really cannot overstate how far they had to go; Cambridge was, and is, a very white place.

Arday had a Ph.D. in education, but only a modest publication record, and he’d been bouncing from one university to another. We know that among the people competing with Arday for the position were two more experienced women of color. But Arday was the only Black applicant. He also had this remarkable back story of being diagnosed early with autism, not speaking until very late, and overcoming that to make a name for himself. And Cambridge was promoting that too.

Part of the issue here is that universities increasingly want to hire stars who have amazing personal stories and big followings that can gain the institution positive media coverage.

But that back story wasn’t true?

Parts of it were true, and parts of it really stretched belief and turned out to be lies and exaggerations. He said he didn’t speak before he was 11 and he didn’t read before he was 18. In our reporting, we found people who knew him as a child, including a speech professional who worked with him, who contradicted this.

Could the hiring committee have realized this?

The short answer is yes. We don’t have full insight into how those deliberations went, but the nine people on the hiring committee were experts on things like how people learn and develop.

At least one key member of the committee was a child psychiatrist who had himself done research on autism. He was arguably in a position to understand that Arday’s claims really had no precedent in medical literature.

Why did they seemingly turn a blind eye?

Cambridge is one of the world’s most elite universities. But it also has a reputation for being very white, privileged and a little stuffy.

So critics say Arday’s backers thought his hire could potentially help change Cambridge’s image. Not only had they hired a Black scholar but also a young scholar who had this remarkable life. It provided a counterpoint to how many people thought about Cambridge at the time.

When did Cambridge first find out about potential problems in Arday’s work?

Almost immediately. Cambridge was first alerted to possible plagiarism three months after he was hired. They didn’t deal with these allegations swiftly, which isn’t unusual. What is unusual is how actively they defended Arday. They said he was facing several issues at the time he wrote those papers that had influenced his work, including direct and indirect racism.

Cambridge then got alerted by a very respected academic industry publication to issues in Arday’s doctoral thesis. But the university continued to defend him, saying at one point that he was the victim of a vile campaign.

So these latest allegations didn’t come out of nowhere. They’ve been circulating inside Cambridge for three years. Cambridge could have easily done its own investigation, but it didn’t.

So Cambridge wasn’t just defending Jason Arday. It was also defending itself, and its initial decision to hire him.

Another concern of other professors my colleagues and I spoke to was that this was a position that typically goes to people who are very senior. By thrusting Arday into that position pretty early in his career, and by heavily promoting his personal story with all its flaws, they argue, the university set him up for intense scrutiny — and ultimately for failure.

That’s not to say that he wasn’t pushing these things himself. But without the Cambridge brand and without that extensive media coverage, his story might have looked very different. And arguably had Cambridge dealt with it earlier, this would not have all blown up in this very public and tragic way.

Do you think the scale of the media attention on Arday was disproportionate for what he did?

Well, I haven’t done an analysis that can speak to that. Arday’s defenders would say that Black academics are subjected to disproportionate scrutiny; they’d cite former Harvard president Claudine Gay, who was accused of plagiarism for much more minor infractions.

But the media is also fascinated by fabulists. Remember George Santos, Jayson Blair or — to give another U.K. example — “The Salt Path”? And this story came with an extra layer of culture war issues around neurodiversity, D.E.I., higher education. It was always going to make for an explosive mix.

What will the long-term fallout of this be, Mara?

At Cambridge, scholars say they’re worried it’s done immense damage to diversity efforts, to the reputation of the university, to their own reputations, and to the recruitment of faculty and students in the future.

Experts on developmental delays worry that the story of Arday’s remarkable trajectory has given families false hope and false expectations of what’s possible with a relatively extreme diagnosis.

And now that he’s died, people are calling for an examination of the media’s role in his death. This story is not over.

Read Mara’s story.

MIDDLE EAST

Israel struck a seaside cafe in Gaza City yesterday, killing at least seven people, including a child, according to a hospital official.

The Israel military also carried out airstrikes on a defunct military air base in Syria, drawing criticism from the U.S.

Potentially damaging U.S. tariffs on Canadian products were put on hold for three days at the 11th hour. Trump claimed that a trade deal was near, Prime Minister Mark Carney was less definitive.

Ugly is subjective. But in this competition, which promotes dog adoptions, it really matters. Last week, a 6-year-old pug who was rescued in the mountains of South Korea won first place. She likes to dip her floppy tongue into everyone’s food bowls and scream at her own reflection in the mirror, according to her biography.

Diya Joukani captures slice-of-life moments in her popular online videos, in which she strolls around Mumbai, drinks from a coconut, skateboards and sips chai with street vendors. Her signature look: wavy hair that falls below her waist and stylish clothes that she designed herself.

The videos have earned her the reputation as “the cool girl from India” and feature people Joukani has known for years: tractor drivers, chai vendors, a potter and others in her neighborhood. Read more and see for yourself.

In the picturesque French Provençal village of Ansouis, a feud between old nobility and new money has brought life to a standstill.

For the third time in six years, the mayor has closed a road under an arched bridge that connects the village’s two halves, snarling traffic and choking businesses at the height of tourist season. He cited structural dangers. But many residents see it as part of his personal vendetta against the wealthy couple who bought his family’s medieval castle and rely on the bridge to reach it. item.title: Send Us Your Questions About the Iran War
item.description:
The United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, starting a monthslong war that has spread to neighboring countries, halted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and rattled the global economy.

The war was not, at least at first, about the strait. Tankers and other ships sailed freely there before the war. In launching strikes, President Trump cited Iran’s nuclear program and a desire to topple the theocratic regime. Since then, his efforts to end the war have faltered, mostly around the question of how to get Iran to open up the strait.

As the conflict nears the six-month mark, we want to hear from our readers.

What questions do you have about the state of the war? Are you concerned about its impact near you? Are you wondering about the options for Washington, Tehran or even other countries in the region? Send us your questions, and we will take them to our correspondents in the Middle East, Washington and elsewhere.

We’ll pick a few questions for our reporters to answer in The World. If we decide to publish your question, we’ll reach out to you.

item.title: Queen Camilla Says It Was ‘Difficult’ to Keep Charles’s Cancer a Secret
item.description:
In a video released on Wednesday, Queen Camilla made rare public comments about King Charles III’s cancer, talking about how difficult his diagnosis had been for her, especially in the days before Buckingham Palace made the news public.

“I was just longing to let it out,” Camilla said in the video, which was released by the British royal family and by a leading U.K. cancer charity, Maggie’s, of which Camilla is the president.

“But, obviously, I couldn’t,” she added.

Camilla was reflecting on a 2024 visit with cancer patients and their families, which she made shortly after Charles’s cancer was diagnosed — but before the palace had made an official announcement.

The queen, who has been involved with Maggie’s for years, had often made such visits. But this time was different, she said: She was there not just as a figurehead, but as another worried spouse.

“I was almost questioning them,” Camilla said. She held back, she said, because she “didn’t want to pry too deeply.”

With Charles’s condition still a secret, she could not tell the others that they were all experiencing the fear and uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis. Holding back was “quite difficult,” she said in the video, which was released to mark the charity’s 30th anniversary.

“I almost said something,” she added, “but I felt that it wasn’t the time.”

It is rare for members of the royal family to speak publicly about their private lives. Since 2024, they have dealt not just with Charles’s diagnosis but with that of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, who announced weeks later that she, too, was battling cancer.

Neither royal has disclosed what type of cancer they have. Both have since returned to public life and have used their diagnoses to advocate for cancer patients and speak about the emotional challenges of facing the disease.

In December, when Charles told the British public that he was doing well and could scale back his treatment, he said it was “a testimony to the remarkable advances that have been made in cancer care in recent years.”

item.title: As Economic Pessimism Spreads, China’s Worker-Writers Strike a Chord
item.description:
A Chinese food delivery driver rushes from gig to gig, measuring time by the number of jobs he completes instead of by the passing of the seasons. He toils in cities across China to send money back to his family, but has been away for so long that his son calls him “that man” instead of “Dad.”

These are scenes from the poems of Wang Jibing, a food delivery driver, one of several Chinese poets and authors who have turned their experiences of repetitive factory labor and insecure gig work into art.

This literary genre has ballooned in popularity in recent years, as many Chinese have grown pessimistic about the economy. For a wide swath of society, wages have stagnated, youth unemployment is high and the promise of a better life in return for hard work has faded. Some authors use their writing to call attention to the harsh realities of life for migrant and gig workers, while others celebrate the humanity that flourishes in spite of those conditions. Their styles are often raw and straightforward.

Writers like Hu Anyan, a courier who wrote a best-selling memoir about the jobs he has worked across the gig economy, and Fan Yusu, who left her children behind to work as a live-in nanny in Beijing, have tapped into these themes. They have published essays online that have been shared widely and led to book deals. Some best-sellers have been translated and published overseas.

Last month, Mr. Wang’s new poetry collection, “Low Flight,” won the Lu Xun Literary Prize, in the highest institutional recognition for the genre yet.

For the Chinese public, curiosity about these workers is intertwined with anxiety about their own prospects. The concern may be particularly pronounced for members of China’s middle class. They “pay more attention to these kinds of narratives because they may represent their future lives,” said Zhu Ping, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of California San Diego’s literature department.

Gig and factory workers are ubiquitous, yet the hardship and indignities they endure are rarely depicted by China’s state-controlled media, which prefers a more positive spin. As the literary work’s influence has grown, Chinese officials, wary of the power of workers’ grievances to illuminate policy shortcomings or spawn unrest, have increasingly sought to shape it, experts said.

The genre known as migrant workers’ literature mirrors the trajectory of a work force that now numbers more than 400 million people.

Since the 1980s, rural workers have powered China’s factories and cities while often being denied the health insurance, unemployment and retirement benefits available to urban residents. The literary movement’s early authors wrote essays and poems about their experiences in factories, but as manufacturing jobs have begun to disappear, its new breakout stars are more often doing gig work.

One such star is Mr. Hu, the courier who wrote a best-selling memoir. The book, “I Deliver Parcels in Beijing,” was published in 2023 in China, where it was deemed that year’s best book by Douban, China’s equivalent to Goodreads. It is a diaristic account of the 19 jobs he held over two decades across China, including as a sorter at a logistics company, security guard, convenience store worker and courier.

Mr. Hu’s work first came to public attention through an essay he posted online. It detailed his year on the night shift sorting packages at a logistics firm, where the work was grueling and he struggled to get used to sleeping during the day:

I passed by a row of houses on my way in every day. I could smell the cooking going on inside, see the people collapsed on their couches, tired and content after a day’s work. That, to me, was what true happiness looked like. Meanwhile I was already more exhausted than those people, and I hadn’t even reached the warehouse. I cursed myself in those moments: My damned body cursed my willpower, and my damned willpower cursed it back. I swore I would go right to sleep when I clocked off in the morning. But then the morning came around, and everything went the same as the day before. I was trapped in a loop.— “I Deliver Parcels in Beijing,” translated into English by Jack Hargreaves.

Ding Nan, a 35-year-old teacher in Wuhan, said Mr. Hu’s book was the first piece of migrant workers’ literature she had read, and she has since sought out more works in the genre.

She said she was drawn to stories of gig workers because of their constant presence in her own life. “They are the strangers we regularly interact with, but I never knew what their lives were like,” she said.

Some pieces approach the experience with more hope. In his poetry collection, “Low Flight,” Mr. Wang, the delivery driver, celebrates the dignity and resilience of delivery workers:

Who prescribes that with wings spread one must fly high

Low flight is also a flight

With wind rustling like birds’ chirps

And wheels speeding like shooting stars

The meal delivery note attached to a takeout

In clear black and white symbolizes urgency

Like a legal document and a magic incantation— “Low Flight,” translated by Chen Du and Xisheng Chen

Ms. Ding said that migrant workers’ stories also changed her preconceptions about the workers. “Society has many stereotypes about them — we think their lives are wretched, that they are oppressed,” she said. “But when I read these books, I realized they are also very optimistic.”

“Low Flight” won Mr. Wang the Lu Xun prize, which is overseen by a government body and given out once every three years. Chinese state media has celebrated Mr. Wang’s win as heralding a new, utopian literary landscape in which anyone can find success.

But a tension exists between the interests of the Chinese government, which downplays stories of poverty or social inequality, and migrant workers’ literature, which lays those realities bare, said Ms. Zhu of the University of California San Diego. She saw Mr. Wang’s award as part of the government’s effort to shape the genre by elevating a more acceptable voice — one that tended toward hope and optimism, rather than criticism of the system’s inherent unfairness.

The Chinese government has said that it wants to foster workers’ voices as part of what it describes as “new literature and arts of the masses,” stories that have taken off in the online era, unconstrained by the traditional gatekeepers of the publishing industry.

That means more resources and opportunities for writers — but largely for the ones who tell palatable stories, said Maghiel van Crevel, a professor of Chinese literature at Leiden University in the Netherlands who studies migrant workers’ literature. Depictions of hardship are acceptable, he said, but linking that hardship to government policy “would be crossing a red line and make it impossible to publish.”

But Mr. van Crevel noted that receiving institutional support did not necessarily mean that a writer had “sold out.” Mr. Wang’s reception by the Chinese establishment “doesn’t necessarily make his writing less authentic,” he said.

Authors like Zheng Xiaoqiong have continued to speak out about workers’ rights even after achieving mainstream success.

Ms. Zheng rose to prominence in China in the 2000s for her poems chronicling the monotony and exhaustion women endured in factories. She described exploitative bosses, workers who suffered from severed fingers or occupational diseases and young women forced into prostitution:

the flowing products and interlocking time are swallowed up quickly

aging ten years flowing past like water enormous weariness

floats through the mind for many years she’s stuck by

the screws one screw two screws turning to the left to the right

fixing her dreams and her youth to some product look

at her pale youth running from an inland village

to a factory by the sea all the way to a shelf in America— “Woman Worker: Youth Pinned to a Station,” translated by Eleanor Goodman.

Ms. Zheng has received literary prizes and parlayed her writing into a better life and a magazine career. She has also continued to speak out about the issues facing workers in China and around the world.

“I’ve always hoped that those in China who have been fortunate enough to achieve upward social mobility can look back and offer a hand to those who are still bogged down, just as they once were,” she said in an interview.

“We cannot change reality with poetry,” she said, “but we have a responsibility to speak out.”

Siyi Zhao contributed research.

item.title: How the Iran War Made Africa’s Richest Man Even Richer
item.description:
Africa’s wealthiest man, Aliko Dangote, is more than $5 billion richer these days, and he partly has the war in Iran to thank for his new windfall.

Mr. Dangote, 69, made much of his fortune in Nigeria by manufacturing basics, such as salt, sugar and cement. Now, the engine driving his wealth is his new $20 billion oil refinery in Lagos, which has seen a spike in demand for petroleum products — both in Africa and elsewhere — since the war began in February.

Despite having abundant crude oil, Africa still relies heavily on imported fuel. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and tankers have choked off Russian supplies to the continent. Oil flows from Europe and the Persian Gulf have also dropped sharply since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries up to one-fifth of the world’s oil supply.

Prices for food, fertilizer and fuel have soared as a consequence, pushing some of Africa’s most vulnerable populations deeper into poverty. But Mr. Dangote and his company have been a rare exception to the rule. And his refinery, which became fully operational just weeks before the U.S. bombed Iran, is doing big business.

Jet fuel shipments from the Dangote Refinery reached the U.S. market for the first time ever this year, according to the company. The Dangote Refinery was “the world’s single largest exporter of jet fuel” in April and May, said Daniel Evans, a vice president of S&P Global Energy, a market-research firm. Last month, the refinery was Europe’s largest supplier of jet fuel and diesel, according to Devakumar Edwin, a vice president of Dangote Industries.

On Tuesday, Dangote Refinery said it had secured $1 billion in financial backing from a Dubai-based investment group to go public on the Nigerian stock exchange. If the listing goes through, it will be Africa’s largest-ever public offering.

“When the war broke out, traders and governments from all around the world — especially in Africa — started calling us for supplies,” said Mr. Edwin. “The crude oil prices have gone up, but the product prices have increased a lot more.”

Nearly two dozen African nations produce crude oil. But the vast majority of the continent’s nearly nine million barrels a day is exported for refining. Most of the domestic refineries, the majority of them state-owned, are dormant.

Nigeria in recent years, for example, has poured several billions of dollars into rehabilitating its three state-run refineries. Not a single one is currently operational.

When the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28, many African nations found themselves in desperate need of petroleum products and scrambling to secure supplies.

East Africa got more than 65 percent of its refined petroleum products from the Middle East last year. By April this year, nearly a third of the gas stations in Kenya had run dry, said Matthew Tracey-Cook, a senior analyst at Platts.

“When the Iran war broke out, the Dangote Refinery was a lifeline to buyers who previously depended on the Persian Gulf for oil products,” said Mr. Tracey-Cook.

When European jet fuel import supplies were choked off by Iran, Mr. Dangote’s refinery began exporting to countries in the Mediterranean and Europe, he added. The Dangote facility has also become a key supplier of diesel and jet fuel to South Africa, a country with close ties to Iran that has historically been dependent on the Middle East for its oil products, Mr. Tracey-Cook said.

Mr. Dangote’s is not the only company in Africa benefiting from the conflict. On Togo’s Atlantic coast is the Port of Lomé, West Africa’s only deepwater port and one of the few on the continent.

The facility, which was built a few years ago with hundreds of millions of dollars of investment from the Mediterranean Shipping Company, a Swiss company, has now taken over a bigger share of the regional energy trade.

Tankers that load fuel from the Dangote refinery in Lagos sail along the West African coast to Lomé, where they offload their cargo onto smaller vessels for onward delivery to markets across the continent.

“The Lomé port is one of the biggest winners from the impact of the disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz,” said Cham Etienne Bama, an analyst.

“Before touching down, the few minutes that we were hanging in air, at the airport, I captured images of vessels at the port,” he said, recalling the crowded vista on a recent trip to Lomé. “It was like you’re looking at the sky in the night,” he said, seeing “so many stars.”

At home in Nigeria, Mr. Dangote has long been criticized as a monopolist and he has come under even more intense scrutiny since fully opening his refinery.

Nigerians had hoped that the refinery would end their reliance on imported fuel and bring down costs. But fuel prices in Nigeria have only surged.

Deji Adeyanju, a human rights lawyer who describes himself as one of the few people in Nigeria willing to criticize Mr. Dangote publicly, said the billionaire has undue influence on the government and benefits from favorable treatment.

Mr. Dangote has long accused the Nigerian government of choking the flow of crude oil, allowing regulators to maintain their grip on Nigeria’s oil business. Regulators have denied any wrongdoing.

Buoyed by his latest windfall, Mr. Dangote is seeking to double the production capacity at his refinery, said Mr. Edwin.

Earlier this month, President William Ruto of Kenya confirmed an agreement with Mr. Dangote to establish a $17 billion refinery in Kenya. The company plans to build a pipeline that will cut across 11 African countries, said Mr. Edwin.

“We will supply Africa,” he said.

item.title: After Drone Strike, a Famed Cathedral in Ukraine Stirs Back to Life
item.description:
There was a bustle on a recent morning on the quiet grounds of Kyiv’s oldest monastery, as volunteers gathered beside Orthodox priests with hoes and rakes to assist in a grand clean up.

Mostly parishioners, military veterans and charity workers, the volunteers had answered a call from the head of the monastery after a Russian drone struck the Dormition Cathedral, at the center of the monastic complex, in June.

It is unclear whether the drone, which was part of a broader bombardment of Ukraine’s capital, had intentionally targeted the cathedral. Still, the strike damaged one of its golden domes and set the roof ablaze.

“I cried when I saw the Dormition Cathedral was on fire,” said Olha Mukha, an economics teacher and parishioner who lives nearby and came to help. “For our enemy, there are no sacred places,” she said.

The cathedral is part of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra preserve, an extensive complex of churches, monastic buildings and ancient catacombs perched above the Dnipro River. The preserve is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a revered place of pilgrimage.

The volunteers gathered last month to clean up the site ahead of its 975th anniversary, which President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and other dignitaries celebrated on Saturday.

Founded in the 11th century, the monastery was home to 1,000 monks at its height and drew patrons among royalty, politicians and pilgrims. Its catacombs house underground churches and the bodies and relics of 120 saints.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the monastery became the center of a standoff between dozens of resident monks who follow the Moscow Orthodox patriarchate, and Ukrainian monks who adhere to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine, which split off in 2018.

Abbot Makariy, 45, who leads the nearby monastery of St. Theodosius and who is set on claiming the entire preserve for the Ukrainian church, was one of the first on the scene on the night of the Russian strike. He recorded his dismay as he filmed the conflagration with his cellphone from an adjacent bell tower. The footage went viral, sparking global outrage and sympathy.

He also filmed as he ran into the burning church. “There was nobody there: no firefighters, nobody,” he recalled. His voice in the footage relayed shock: “Poor Dormition,” he said as he filmed. “Everything is burning.”

The devastation was particularly painful, he said, because of the effort that had gone into building the cathedral. It was leveled to the ground in 1941 during World War II and was rebuilt only in 2000, after the Soviet Union fell and Ukraine gained independence.

In June, the cathedral escaped major destruction. The strike tore chunks of brick out of the masonry and set the roof ablaze, but emergency workers prevented the flames from spreading, officials at the complex said. Another drone passed overhead that night and struck an 18th century fortress and former arsenal across the road.

On a recent visit, the cathedral roof was encased in plastic sheeting and the windows of its cupolas were boarded up. A burning smell lingered in the dimly lit interior, as portable fans whirred at full speed to dry out walls that had been soaked by firefighters’ hoses.

The ornate iconostasis, a gilded screen — the largest in Ukraine — concealing the sanctuary, survived intact. Priests rescued valuable artifacts, icons and religious utensils, including a heavy silver coffin encasing a relic of St. Stephen, which is now in a nearby museum building, museum officials said.

Ivan Yahovenko, a deputy director at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra preserve, said Ukraine’s culture ministry was considering plans to build a stronger roof covering to protect the cathedral from snow through the winter. Reconstruction work would depend on funding, he said.

But even as air raid sirens and explosions sounded in Kyiv, Abbot Makariy was moving on, intent on readying the cathedral and the preserve for the anniversary event.

“We are going to open the catacombs for the first time in three years, and there is a big mess down there,” he said last month, ahead of the clean up.

With only 30 monks in his monastery, he had appealed to volunteers, among them military veterans who have been encouraged to use the space as a refuge and place of healing. Over three days, they cut and cleared overgrown gardens and courtyards and weeded the cobbled pathways.

Petro Hadzhala, 22, a novice priest and chorister, was among those helping. “Maybe it was God’s will,” he said of the strike. “Maybe we need a sign to tell us that we have an enemy and we need to unite under one church and one country.”

Parishioners laid out plates of sandwiches for lunch. Then teams of women armed with buckets and mops set about cleaning the cathedral, some climbing up to the choir gallery and others mopping the marble floor over and over.

“This is an incredibly difficult time for all of us,” said Liudmyla Balashova, 56, a director at a textile firm in Kyiv, who paused to say a prayer. “We need to prove, perhaps to ourselves above all, that with God’s help we can overcome anything.”

item.title: Chinese Comic Investigated After Singing a Riff of a Patriotic Song
item.description:
Ad-libbing during a routine is standard for many comedians. But in China, it can land performers in hot water. That was the case for one of the country’s most famous comics, Guo Degang, who is under official investigation for riffing on the lyrics of a famous patriotic song during a show.

Mr. Guo has drawn comparisons to the likes of Ricky Gervais, and has starred in movies and hosted TV shows in China. After a show in Wuhan in July, he was reported to city’s culture and tourism bureau for singing a modified version of the song, which hails the bravery of Chinese soldiers during a historic battle against Japan.

His case highlights the delicate line comedians must tread in a heavily censored creative landscape. The comedy scene provides a rare venue for indirect criticisms about contemporary life in China; but the space for self-expression is becoming increasingly narrow as China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, has made arts and culture a focus for ideological crackdowns.

The bureau launched an investigation into Mr. Guo last week after receiving a complaint, according to The Paper, a popular Shanghai-based state-backed newspaper. The bureau said it was looking into whether he had violated a regulation under which performers must have their sets vetted by officials in advance, the outlet reported.

An official who answered the phone at the Hubei Culture and Tourism Bureau, in the province encompassing Wuhan, confirmed the investigation against Mr. Guo on Tuesday. He described the matter as sensitive, but did not provide more details. A show Mr. Guo was scheduled to perform in the city of Xi’an was postponed, according to a social media post by the theater that was going to host it. Organizers have not announced if it will be rescheduled.

Mr. Guo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Guo, 53, is credited with reviving cross talk, or xiangsheng, a comedy genre that mixes scripted and improvised sketches that originated in the Qing dynasty. In the 2010s, Chinese media lauded him for attracting younger audiences to a genre with an aging fan base.

But improvisation can be at odds with official policy, which requires comics to submit scripts and set lists of their performances for official approval in advance. In recent years, Mr. Xi has stepped up controls on speech that challenges the Communist Party’s narratives around politics and history. The government has also demanded that artists align their creative visions with the Party’s goals and has encouraged comics to promote a nationalist vision.

The song Mr. Guo performed in July was “Playing My Beloved Pipa,” which refers to a traditional musical instrument and describes the heroics of Chinese guerrilla fighters against Japanese forces during the second Sino-Japanese war of 1937 to 1945. It was written for a well-known 1950s movie, “Railway Guerrilla,” which shared a name with the Chinese armed forces. In 2019, it was included in a list of 100 songs the Communist Party’s Central Committee named to celebrate the 70th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China.

According to media reports and videos of the performance posted online, Mr. Guo changed a line of lyrics: “The sun is about to set in the west; all is quiet on Weishan Lake.” He replaced the lake with “the Forbidden City,” a Beijing palace that was once the country’s political center. He also added other humorous lines, in which he pretended to pray to Buddha.

Mr. Guo had received the necessary approvals for his performance, but had not indicated that he would be changing the lyrics, The Paper reported, citing Wuhan officials.

Mr. Guo’s case highlighted how the Communist Party is increasingly sensitive to depictions of history that stray from officially sanctioned narratives, said Jian Xu, an associate professor at Deakin University in Melbourne who studies China’s digital culture and celebrity politics. The slander of China’s martyrs and heroes was made a crime in 2021 under an amended criminal code, and has been enforced zealously since. Anything that could be seen as a slight against revolutionary heroes, or classic art and literature that celebrated Communist history, was likely to receive strong public and government condemnation, Mr. Xu said.

In addition, it reflected how “celebrities are increasingly subject to moral governance by both the public and the state and are expected to promote ‘positive energy’ and socially approved values,” Mr. Xu said.

Chinese comedians have come under increasing scrutiny from the government and audiences in recent years. In 2023, a Chinese comedy studio was fined $2 million because Li Haoshi, a popular comedian, compared two stray dogs chasing a squirrel to the military. Announcing that penalty, officials urged artists and writers to have “correct creative thinking” and “provide healthy spiritual nourishment for the people.” Following that episode, comedy clubs around China canceled shows.

Online, some argued that Mr. Guo should be punished because appropriating and satirizing a revolutionary song was a severe matter. But others wondered if the outrage was disproportionate to the scale of his transgression.

Hu Xijin, the former editor of the Communist Party-run Global Times newspaper, said in a social media post that, although he found Mr. Guo’s version of the song “uncomfortable and inappropriate,” he was unsure how severe the matter was. “Those in our arts and literature scene who dare to maliciously cross the line are few and far in between,” he wrote in a post on Weibo, where he has nearly 25 million followers.

“To assume that such people are everywhere, and to give the harshest punishment to anyone who steps out of line to make an example out of them, is an error of judgment,” he added.

Siyi Zhao contributed research.

item.title: At Tree 55, Vietnam’s Gen Z Demands to Hold the Privileged Accountable
item.description:
A young woman in a red hoodie and wide sunglasses stopped her motorbike just past Tree 55 on Nguyen Huy Tu Street in central Hanoi. She snapped a photo with her phone. She stared at the tree again. She lingered with defiance.

No one else was parked there at lunchtime on Tuesday in front of the quiet men in pairs with hints of plainclothes authority — the middle-manager dress shoes, the aviator shades.

Tree 55, as everyone likely knew, was where an 18-year-old student, Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, better known as Mina, had been hit along with her father by a BMW. She died after being thrown from a motorbike just days before her university exams. That was 15 months ago.

I was there this week to see whether flowers would arrive. The bright bouquets teens and twenty-somethings kept delivering, photographing and sharing on social media. The ones the police had recently removed. And if tension hovered in their absence, it was with good reason.

On Monday night, after an eruption of Gen Z outrage and creativity thrust Memorial Tree 55, or “The Tree of Justice,” into the local zeitgeist, Vietnam’s national broadcaster officially confirmed what many had long insisted: A former Communist Party official, Nguyen Sy Cuong, had been behind the wheel of that BMW.

The TV report said Mr. Cuong — who had been vice chairman of the foreign affairs committee in the National Assembly until earlier this year — caused the crash by illegally driving on the wrong side of the road. It also said that he was not prosecuted because he had compensated the victim’s relatives, and they chose not to press charges. The victim’s father, with his face obscured, urged people to move on in the segment, which did not mention that Mr. Cuong’s wife is Vietnam’s minister of culture, sports and tourism.

Their powerful positions, some said, had kept the crash out of public view.

But in a one-party state that Harvard scholars have described as repressive but responsive, the official acknowledgment of responsibility was an extraordinary concession to public pressure. Warning against “opportunists exploiting the incident on social media,” the report reflected the government’s deep concerns about an unexpected youth movement pushing for accountability at a time when officials are focused on economic growth.

Adding to the sensitivity, the collective action comes after Gen Z activists toppled leaders in Nepal, challenged authorities in Indonesia, and continue to rattle the power structure in India.

Hanoi officials had already warned state-run outlets to reduce coverage of the youth-driven “Cockroach” demonstrations rocking New Delhi, according to a written notice shared among reporters. The internal guidance said that the information could be “exploited for anti-government purposes.”

And yet, for now at least, Monday’s careful admissions in TV form show no sign of weakening the resistance to what many see as sloppy propaganda and protection for the powerful.

On Wednesday, legal experts said the victim’s family could not, simply by declining to press charges, determine whether Mr. Cuong would be prosecuted. Online, anonymous critics accused the state broadcaster of using A.I. to doctor a document showing Mr. Cuong had passed a sobriety test. Others questioned if it was really the victim’s father in the report.

Their claims could not be independently verified. The network did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cuong, reached by phone on Wednesday, said only “I am busy, I cannot talk” before hanging up.

By midafternoon, the original version of the news report had disappeared from YouTube.

And all that public anger is about more than the crash. It reflects a broader frustration with corruption, privilege and the mechanisms of secrecy that benefit elites in a fast-changing society that has become more bifurcated by wealth and political connections.

As one commenter wrote on Threads on Wednesday, letting Mr. Cuong sidestep criminal prosecution simply confirms that the country’s legal system “creates loopholes so that the rich can stuff money and power into them, while the poor cannot.”

Fury over who gets to police both behavior and expression has also fueled the backlash. Censorship, in fact, sparked its rise.

On July 31, a rapper known as MCK announced that he would scrub digital platforms of several songs that cultural authorities had deemed vulgar from his new hit album.

That’s when Mr. Cuong’s wife, Lam Thi Phuong Thanh, the minister of culture since April, became a target of especially intense curiosity.

Within days of MCK’s cleanup, Threads lit up with questions about why there was so little information made public about the crash on May 25, 2025, involving her husband.

On Aug. 12, Luat Khoa, an independent Vietnamese news outlet run by former reporters for state-run media who have mostly left the country, reported that Nguyen Sy Cuong had become one of the platform’s top topics, with more than 1 million posts related to the accident.

The next day, a Facebook page about Vietnamese politics posted an announcement saying that the authorities had requested that Facebook “continuously block three of my posts about Nguyen Sy Cuong.”

Then security video from a nearby building surfaced and started to spread online.

It showed the BMW, an SUV, smashing into the tree with a motorbike against its grill. A man gets out, seemingly uninjured, and can be seen approaching where Mina and her father have been thrown. A woman bearing a strong resemblance to Ms. Thanh emerges from the passenger side as a crowd gathers. She heads away from the scene, comes back to collect something from the front seat, then walks away.

In the brief clip, neither driver nor passenger rushed to help the wounded.

Another eruption of social media outrage followed, with some quoting “Animal Farm,” and “The Hunger Games,” accusing Ms. Thanh of trying to protect herself and her husband after online takedown orders spread to more posts.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Threads, did not respond to a request for comment. Its most recent report on Vietnam shows a rise in censorship, with restrictions placed on more than 5,300 items in the last six months of 2025 in response to requests from the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Public Security.

Undeterred, people found other ways to make their sadness and anger known. They ordered flowers to be delivered to the base of Tree 55. Users posted photos of a growing, colorful pile until the afternoon of Aug. 14, when another set of images made the rounds — showing the bouquets being removed by the police and thrown into a dumpster.

Then the Threads community turned to white ribbons, tying them on backpacks, as symbols of student promise.

Around the same time, someone created a virtual Memorial Tree Number 55.

“Rest in peace down there, sister,” said one of the many notes left at the site. “We Gen-Z will handle everything.”

The government has yet to mention or cut off access to the collection.

Ms. Thanh could not be reached for comment on Wednesday. She and her husband did not appear in the state television report — a point some critics interpreted as a lack of remorse.

In the void, messages of support for Mina and calls for accountability continue to multiply.

Tung Ngo contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Israel Opens Criminal Inquiries Into Killings of Hind Rajab, 6, and of Medics
item.description:
The Israeli military said on Wednesday that it would open criminal investigations into the killing of Palestinians by its troops in two high-profile cases during the war in Gaza, including the deaths of Hind Rajab, a 6-year-old girl, and of more than a dozen medical workers.

The decision to open the criminal investigations into suspicions of military misconduct during the war came after a lengthy review of the cases and followed widespread international condemnation of Israel’s conduct, with several rights groups and governments accusing the country of war crimes.

More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza during the war, according to the territory’s health ministry, whose data does not distinguish between civilians and combatants but has included thousands of children.

The Israeli military said in a statement on Wednesday that a fact-finding mission had completed a review of about 150 incidents during the war, which was waged after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and had transferred them to the military prosecution services for examination. Such investigations have rarely led to convictions.

The first of the two cases to be investigated involves the deaths of Hind Rajab and six members of her family who were killed in a car in Gaza City in January 2024, as well as the shelling of a Palestine Red Crescent ambulance that had tried to approach the vehicle, an attack that caused the deaths of two paramedics.

The second case involves the fatal shooting in March 2025 of 14 Palestinian medics and rescue workers in southern Gaza, as well as that of a U.N. employee who drove by after the others had been shot.

The military said that it had found no grounds for criminal investigation in three other cases, including the killing of seven employees of World Central Kitchen, a relief group, in April 2024. The military also declined to open a criminal investigation into a deadly strike on a building occupied by Doctors Without Borders in February 2024 or into the killing of two of the medical organization’s employees who were traveling in a convoy in Gaza City in November 2023.

Natan Odenheimer contributed reporting.

item.title: U.A.E. Halts Trade Ties With Iran and Says It Was Targeted With Missiles
item.description:
The United Arab Emirates said it is halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran, increasing economic pressure on the Islamic Republic, hours after accusing Iran of launching ballistic missiles toward the Emirates.

The decision was made “in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security,” Afra Al Hameli, a spokeswoman for the Emirati Foreign Ministry, said in a statement late on Tuesday. She added that the Emirates was “firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.”

The Emirates, located just 50 miles from Iran across the Persian Gulf, has nurtured close economic and cultural ties with the Islamic Republic for decades, despite political tensions between the two countries.

The Emirati city of Dubai has long been a major trade hub for Iran, and analysts say it has been key to Iranian efforts to evade sanctions — a fact that has often elicited complaints and pressure from American authorities. Emirati officials say that they crack down on any sanctions violations when they find them.

The Emirati government statement did not specify what prompted its announcement, nor did it make it clear when the decision to halt trade was implemented. But over the past week, the Emirates has accused Iran of attacking Emirati oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway on Iran’s southern coast that is a key transit route for oil and gas shipping.

And on Tuesday, the Emirati Defense Ministry issued warnings of an incoming missile attack, later saying that two ballistic missiles launched from Iran had targeted maritime aviation. Iran denied carrying out those attacks, and has neither denied nor claimed responsibility for the recent tanker strikes.

The decision to halt trade with Iran was announced hours after a call from President Trump to the Emirati ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed.

After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, setting off a regional conflagration, the Emirates bore the initial brunt of Iran’s retaliation. The Emirates, which hosts a major American military base, reported more than 2,700 ballistic missile and drone attacks from Iran.

After the United States and Iran reached an initial cease-fire agreement in April, tensions between the Emirates and Iran had eased significantly, with direct contact between senior officials and the resumption of flights between the two countries.

As the truce has frayed in the months since, Iran largely focused its attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, sparing the Emirates.

The recent attacks on Emirati oil tankers have elicited a strong condemnation from the Emirati government, and on Saturday, the Emirati Foreign Ministry accused Iran of targeting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as “a tool of economic coercion or blackmail” that constituted a “direct threat to the stability of the region.”

In a call on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Emirates’ national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, discussed “U.S.-UAE coordination to hold Iran and its terrorist proxies accountable for ongoing attacks,” according to a state department spokesman, Tommy Pigott.

The Emirati Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the motivation and timing of its decision.

Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting from London.

item.title: Tariffs on Hold as Trump Claims Deal With Canada Is Near
item.description:
Canada got a three-day reprieve on damaging new American tariffs against billions of goods, with President Trump claiming that a deal was close but Prime Minister Mark Carney saying only that substantial progress had been made.

Mr. Trump announced the delay on imposing 50 percent tariffs in a social media post on Tuesday night, roughly 90 minutes before the midnight deadline. The White House issued a proclamation saying Canada had agreed to make certain trade concessions, and the extra days were needed to finalize those provisions.

“I have paused the 50% Tariffs against Canada, that were scheduled to kick in tomorrow morning for a three day period, based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL!” Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump has previously announced deals with other countries, only to have them fall through — including a recent series of elapsed agreements with Iran. In a brief statement, Mr. Carney was less definitive about what the talks have produced.

“Over the last number of weeks, Canada has engaged in intensive discussions with the United States to address outstanding trade issues,” he said. “Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done.”

Reflecting his pivot away from Canada’s economic dependence on the United States, Mr. Carney added: “Canada remains focused on building a stronger, more independent, and more competitive economy at home.”

In a social media post, the Office of the United States Trade Representative, which was carrying out the negotiations, said the deal would “include comprehensive market access for all American goods, economic security commitments, digital trade alignment” and other provisions that would protect the U.S. market.

Entering the negotiations, Mr. Carney said that he was attempting to avert the new tariffs, which, if put in place, would affect hundreds products that account, by the Trump administration’s estimates, for $20 billion in Canadian exports.

Mr. Carney said last month that “our objective is not to reach a deal whatever it costs” with the United States. But he has also made it clear that Canada would make any agreement contingent on eliminating or reducing tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos introduced last year. Canada also is seeking relief on tariffs against Canadian lumber that date back decades and were increased by Mr. Trump.

The United States, in turn, was looking for an end to the boycotts of American wine and spirits in some provincial alcohol distribution systems that followed Mr. Trump’s earlier tariffs. It was also seeking an end to Canada’s retaliatory tariffs against imports of American automobiles and changes to how some American dairy products are allowed to enter Canada’s largely closed market. In the presidential proclamation, Mr. Trump claimed that Canada had “expressed a commitment” to address all those issues.

Mr. Trump linked the looming agreement to the Keystone XL, a major pipeline project that would have transported oil from Canada to the United States Gulf Coast, but was scrapped by the Biden administration in 2021. The project had been approved during the first Trump administration.

“The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!” Mr. Trump added on his social media post.

Despite being considered largely dead for five years, speculation that a new project, closely mirroring Keystone XL, could return grew this year as a U.S. company filed an application in Montana to build a pipeline bringing in Canadian oil.

The trade talks have been a prelude to a larger negotiation, over the future of the North American trade agreement. The United States and Mexico have carried out several rounds of talks over the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which Mr. Trump signed in his first term, but has since started to criticize. For U.S. officials, the threat of tariffs has been a way to amass negotiating leverage over the Canadian government, while also forcing Canada to act on trade issues they deem unfair.

While Mr. Carney has pulled back some of Canada’s trade retaliation and made other concessions to the United States, he has seemed far less willing to discuss giving anything more to the United States since Mr. Trump announced the sweeping 50 percent tariffs in July.

Since his return to office, Mr. Trump has started a trade war with Canada that has shredded free-trade agreements going back to 1989 while stoking anger and fear among Canadians. In Canada, frustrations have been expressed in a various ways, including a drastic decline in vacation travel by Canadians to the United States.

In a poll by Abacus Data released on Monday, 74 percent of respondents said that American trade actions had already affected their households, with 30 percent describing the effects as “major.”

While the Supreme Court struck down most of Mr. Trump’s tariffs in February, the steel, aluminum and auto tariffs against Canada were brought under another law that was not covered by that decision. The tariffs now on hold were to be made under another law, an untested trade provision from 1930.

A conversation between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney resumed trade talks in late July. The United States broke off negotiations last fall on steel, aluminum and autos after the province of Ontario placed television ads in the United States that featured clips of President Ronald Reagan, who signed the 1989 free trade agreement with Canada, warning about the dangers of tariffs.

News of the three-day reprieve brought some relief in Canada, but industry leaders highlighted that the prolonged uncertainty was damaging.

“Let’s be clear: the tariff delay provides relief on both sides of the border,” Candace Laing, who leads the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, said in a statement. “Businesses may not be closing up shop with this news, but an extension doesn’t bring the certainty that a signed interim deal would,” she added.

In the United States, the chance of a breakthrough on some Canadian measures was eagerly anticipated. In a statement, Chris Swonger, the president of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, said he appreciated Mr. Trump’s effort to restore access for American spirits after more than a year and a half of sales bans.

“These provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70 percent, leaving American distillers caught in the middle of a broader trade dispute,” he said.

item.title: Ukraine’s Ex-Defense Minister Calls for Election, Cementing Break With Zelensky
item.description:
Ukraine’s popular former defense minister has called for wartime elections in Ukraine, setting up a potential confrontation with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the man who fired him last month.

After Russia invaded in February 2022, elections in Ukraine were suspended under martial law. Opposing political parties and some Ukrainians have grumbled about Mr. Zelensky’s hold on power, which has extended for more than seven years, but rallied behind him because of the war.

The first major crack in that largely unified front appeared on Tuesday evening, when the former defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, whose firing prompted sustained protests against Mr. Zelensky, posted a nine-minute video on social media. In it, Mr. Fedorov argued that Ukraine was facing a systemic crisis of governance.

Ukrainians, Mr. Fedorov said, need to be able to exercise their democratic rights despite the war with Russia. He did not directly put himself forward as a candidate to succeed Mr. Zelensky. But the video of Mr. Fedorov, dressed in a black military-style shirt, dramatically spotlighted at a wooden desk, had the feel of a campaign declaration.

“Can Russia effectively be given the right to dictate when Ukrainians can choose their government again?” Mr. Fedorov said. “I am convinced that the answer is no. Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. We are fighting precisely because we want to remain a free European state.”

Mr. Zelensky, a onetime comic actor who rose to prominence playing an accidental president of Ukraine who fought corruption and government waste, was elected in the spring of 2019.

He and other Ukrainian leaders have argued that it is impossible to hold safe and fair wartime elections. The law could be changed to allow elections before the war ends, but it is unclear how voting would be conducted for soldiers, for Ukrainians who fled to other countries and for those who are in frontline cities under constant Russian bombardment.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has seized on the lack of elections to call Mr. Zelensky an illegitimate president, even as Russia itself remains far from a democratic paragon.

President Trump and his inner circle have occasionally echoed the Russian talking point. In December, Mr. Trump said it was time for presidential elections in Ukraine. In response, Mr. Zelensky said he was ready.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Despite rumors of elections this year, nothing has materialized. Any pressure from the Trump administration has dwindled as Washington has become consumed by the war against Iran.

Mr. Zelensky has been free to politically neutralize any potential challengers. The popular leader of the Ukrainian Army during the first two years of the war, Gen. Valery Zaluzhny, was practically banished, becoming the Ukrainian ambassador to Britain. The popular leader of military intelligence, Kyrylo Budanov, was named Mr. Zelensky’s chief of staff.

Mr. Fedorov is different. He has not been afraid to criticize Mr. Zelensky publicly after his removal last month.

At 35, Mr. Fedorov is the face of a younger, tech-savvy generation. As minister of digital transformation, he tried to make it easier for soldiers to purchase the drones they needed and to adapt military strategies based on the troves of data produced in the war.

In January, Mr. Fedorov was named defense minister. Under his leadership, the ministry intensified a push for machine-led warfare and for an approach to war that relied more on data and statistics. In the first months of the year, Ukraine’s military started to fare better than it had in years.

Even as Mr. Fedorov’s popularity soared, he clashed with the military’s occasionally sclerotic old guard, including the army’s top commander, Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi. Mr. Fedorov also drew intense pushback from Ukraine’s entrenched defense contractors, he has said, as he tried to revamp procurement and to combat corruption.

Mr. Zelensky, continuing a pattern of sidelining anyone who becomes too politically popular, fired Mr. Fedorov on July 15 after days of rumors of a government shake-up.

Daily protests against Mr. Zelensky then began, with demonstrators calling for Mr. Fedorov’s reinstatement and for the firing of General Syrskyi. Unlike other potential rivals who have lost their positions but stayed in the Zelensky fold, Mr. Fedorov refused any other job offer. The only position he would accept, he said, was defense minister.

In the fallout, Mr. Zelensky replaced General Syrskyi but seemingly weathered the political crisis. Parliament was on recess. The daily protests grew smaller.

Still, on Sunday evening, shortly before the Ukrainian Parliament was set to return and one month after Mr. Fedorov was ousted, thousands showed up at a demonstration. They sang Ukrainian songs and shouted slogans including, “The people are the power,” “Corruption kills” and, simply, “Fedorov.”

On Tuesday evening, Mr. Zelensky submitted a proposal to Parliament to appoint Yevhenii Khmara, who had run the domestic intelligence agency, as the new defense minister. Mr. Fedorov then posted his video.

Hours before a scheduled vote on the defense minister pick, Ukrainian anti-corruption agencies announced a special investigation into a group of lawmakers and “high-ranking officials” from Mr. Zelensky’s office, the latest accusation of graft to rattle his inner circle.

Yurii Shyvala, Constant Méheut and Oleksandra Mykolyshyn contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: With Limited Options, Trump Tries Economic Pressure on Iran — Again
item.description:
Iran has survived harsh U.S. sanctions since 1979. It is betting it can endure even more.

In the 47 years since the Islamic Revolution, the United States has taken step after step to isolate the country with only a brief reprieve after the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, which President Trump excoriated and abandoned in 2018.

Mr. Trump promised “maximum pressure” then, and now, with limited military options, threatens even more. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned last week of “never before seen” measures — perhaps, analysts suggest, secondary sanctions on countries like China that buy Iranian oil, or further penalties on financial transactions.

Iran is more likely to step up attacks on American allies in the Persian Gulf than to surrender its hold on the Strait of Hormuz, analysts said. “Iran’s economy is in serious trouble, but it is not collapsing,” said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli expert on Iran. “More importantly, the regime is likely to escalate before it capitulates.”

U.S. and international sanctions and economic pressure did help lead to the 2015 nuclear deal, when the supreme leader then, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, authorized negotiations to limit Iran’s nuclear program in return for frozen assets and sanction relief.

Since Mr. Trump withdrew from the deal and imposed more sanctions, Iran has adjusted to a high level of economic disruption, developing sophisticated smuggling routes and new markets, particularly for oil. For now, Iran insists on maintaining effective control of the strait while the American Navy continues to blockade it. A few ships are slipping through, but traffic is down more than 90 percent from before the war.

Iran’s economy is badly damaged, hurting ordinary people, but its leaders have shown, through brutal crackdowns on protest and dissent, that they are relatively unconcerned with public opinion.

Having survived what it once feared — an Israeli-American war against it — a more military-minded and authoritarian Islamic Republic has itself doubled down. Esmail Baghaei, the spokesman for the foreign ministry, said on Monday that new measures would have “no effect on Iran’s position.”

Economic pressure will only succeed if “our resilience is greater than that of the Iranian regime, and it’s not clear that’s a good bet,” said Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert and director of foreign policy at the Brookings Institution. “Iran’s economy has been shaped by U.S. economic pressure.”

Iran’s economy is suffering, without question, but gradually, while the regime keeps a stranglehold on any popular protest.

Since the war began in earnest in February, the Iranian economy and its industrial sector have been contracting for the first time in eight years, said Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, chief executive of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a research organization based in London.

Iran will face more challenges, from higher inflation to weakness in the job market, he said. “But it won’t lead to a different political outcome.”

Some Iranian leaders, to be sure, are deeply concerned with the economic disaster and support a more rapid diplomatic deal with Washington. But the leadership appears united in retaining effective control over the strait as its best leverage and deterrent against another war.

Iran has adapted to American and international sanctions by increasing its ties to Russia and China. It sells most of its oil at a discount to China, which has ignored international sanctions against the purchase of Iranian oil. It also uses small, independent Chinese refineries, known as “teapots,” that are less exposed to American sanctions.

Iran has developed smuggling networks and a “shadow fleet,” transferring its oil to other ships that can easily disguise its origin. And it has built up its industrial sector and cut back sharply on imports and its use of the dollar, using foreign banks and bartering oil for goods.

Since the war and the American blockade, Iran has been storing oil onshore and in a variety of older tankers, while shipping some of it by road and rail and reducing output on some wells. When the memorandum of understanding with the United States was signed in June and the American blockade was temporarily lifted, Iran used the period of calm assiduously.

Iran had oil already outside the strait to sell before the blockade, and at the outset of the agreement it exported another 80 million barrels before Washington reimposed sanctions and the blockade, easing the pressure on storage, said Brett Erickson of Obsidian Risk Advisors.

Before the war, Iran was exporting about 1.8 million barrels a day. Now, given the increase in the oil price because of the conflict, Iran is ahead of what it budgeted for oil sales for this year, he said.

The exchange rate for the Iranian rial against the dollar is bad, but the speed of depreciation is slowing, as is inflation. If Washington is relying on economic pressure, “you wouldn’t want slower inflation and a lower rial exchange rate than before the war,” Mr. Erickson said.

For the policy to succeed, “we need to push them down quickly, not wait nine more years to collapse them,” he added. “A dagger hurts but doesn’t lop off the head of the enemy.”

Iran is gambling that the closure of the strait will put more pressure on Mr. Trump to blink first and negotiate a deal that Iran can accept. Tehran is counting on increasing economic anxiety from America’s allies to push Mr. Trump back to the table.

The global economy is missing millions of barrels of oil a day and strategic stockpiles, including in Europe and the United States, are badly diminished. Ukraine continues to damage Russia’s refineries, further cutting the amount of oil on the market.

Regionally, key energy producers like Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq and Kuwait are badly hurt by the closure of the strait, and Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Oman have argued in Washington against further military escalation, given Iran’s ability to strike their energy infrastructure.

“In a battle of economic wills it’s very uncertain the West will win,” Ms. Maloney of the Brookings Institution said.

Mr. Trump defends the war as necessary to ensure that Iran can never build a nuclear weapon. But after he abandoned the 2015 nuclear deal, Iran tried to pressure the world with enhanced enrichment that brought it to the edge of being a nuclear-capable military power, even as it denied ever seeking a bomb.

That assurance died with the former supreme leader. His son and successor, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, appears ready for open-ended confrontation with America and is considered by U.S. intelligence to be more flexible about creating a nuclear weapon. In Iran, said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, trust in Mr. Trump is minimal and the 2015 deal is considered “a four-letter word.”

Now, Mr. Trump is offering Iran very little in exchange for opening the Strait of Hormuz, with no U.S. commitment to unfreeze its assets or lift sanctions. “There is no reasonable deal for Iran on the table,” Mr. Nasr said.

“The choice is between total surrender and fighting it out,” he added. “And they have bet that the only way to get a better deal is to accept costs now and hold the global economy’s and Trump’s feet to the fire.”
